 ANDI President Summarizes Colombian Business Leaders’ Views on the 2027 Minimum Wage A 
 By Leon Thompson 
 -
 November 11, 2026 
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... 
 Luz Stella Murgas, New President of the National Association of Business Owners of Colombia (ANDI). Credit: X: @luzstellamurgas 
 For the first time in the history of the National Association of Business Owners of Colombia ( ANDI ), founded in 1944, a woman has been elected to lead it. She is Luz Stella Murgas, a lawyer from Universidad del Rosario and a specialist in Tax Law.
 Among the main challenges of her tenure will be strengthening competitiveness, promoting investment, boosting formal employment, and consolidating dialogue between the public and private sectors. But she will also have a significant influence on the definition of the minimum wage for Colombian workers in 2027.
 Murgas addressed this issue in recent hours, since one of her first tasks as ANDI president will be to participate in the discussions between the National Government, business owners, and labor unions to define the increase workers will receive starting next January 1.
 Two Principles Must Guide the Minimum Wage Discussion
 The business association leader, who worked for eight years at Ecopetrol and later held executive positions at the National Hydrocarbons Agency (ANH), and who has been president of the Colombian Natural Gas Association (Naturgas) since 2021, defended the position that the salary adjustment must follow the traditional formula of inflation plus productivity, thus moving away from increases outside that range, as happened during the previous government.
 “Colombia needs workers to have better incomes, and we also need to protect the source of employment,” Murgas said on Blu Radio. “That discussion about the minimum wage must revolve around those two principles, following the guidelines and criteria established by DANE regarding the CPI and productivity indicators.”
 However, she avoided giving a precise figure for the 2027 wage increase. She explained that ANDI is still holding internal discussions and that the decision must be built together with the other parties participating in the negotiations.
 “The debate cannot be limited at this time to giving a figure or a number,” she added on the same radio station. “It would be very irresponsible of me, because this also requires an agreement with other key actors in defining these increases.”
 Murgas insisted that the country needs a technical, prudent, and responsible discussion, in which the positions of workers, business owners , and other stakeholders are heard. She believes the goal should be to find a formula that makes it possible to improve wages while maintaining companies’ capacity to generate employment.
 She pointed out that better incomes and greater competitiveness must be part of the same solution, although she acknowledged that these are objectives that can compete with each other. “We all want better wages, but we also want greater competitiveness, and that must be part of the same solution,” she maintained.
 Key Dates in the Minimum Wage Discussion
 She also linked the wage discussion to the issues raised in the fiscal adjustment law, considering that economic decisions must be analyzed jointly. ANDI expressed its willingness to participate in the discussions, but Murgas reiterated that it is not yet time to commit to a specific percentage.
 As the days go by, the atmosphere surrounding the minimum wage is heating up. The wage and labor policy negotiation committee must meet next November 18. The Ministry of Labor is considering bringing forward its installation compared with the initial schedule.
 On November 30, DANE and the productivity subcommittee must present the report on total productivity, one of the technical elements used to calculate the minimum wage increase.
 December 15 is the deadline established by law for the Government, business associations, and unions to reach a negotiated agreement. If there is no consensus, additional negotiation and deliberation sessions may be held during the second half of December.
 If the parties fail to reach an agreement, the Government will have until December 30, 2026, to issue the decree establishing the minimum wage increase.
 Projections for Colombia’s Minimum Wage in 2027
 For now, if the traditional formula of inflation plus productivity is taken into account, and considering that October inflation reached 6.30%, a figure to which approximately one percentage point of productivity would be added, the minimum wage increase for 2027 would exceed 7.3%.
 This is only a reference that provides some insight into the issue because no percentage has yet been agreed upon. The productivity report that DANE must present before the installation of the wage negotiation committee on November 18 is still pending.
 However, the October inflation figure has become one of the main reference points for this discussion. The annual variation reached 6.30%, compared with the 5.51% recorded in the same month of 2025, representing an increase of 0.79 percentage points.
 Thus, the projections are based on the current basic salary of 1,750,905 pesos (US$529), not including the transportation allowance, which amounts to 249,095 pesos (US$75). With an 8% adjustment, the basic income would increase by 140,072 pesos (US$42) and reach 1,890,977 pesos (US$571.4). But if the increase were 9%, it would rise by 157,581 pesos (US$47.6), reaching 1,908,486 pesos (US$576.6).
